children: By Ruth Simon | Photography by Alexander Cohn

Nicholas Zingone, age 91, greeted longtime customers streaming into his family's nearly century-old Manhattan grocery on a recent afternoon before ringing up their purchases of bleach, butter, fresh fruit and cans of soda.
J.J. Grabenstein, a customer of 25 years who stopped by to pick up a soda, planned to return later to give medicine to Oliver, the orange tabby cat prowling the store's two overstuffed aisles.
"I've been coming here my entire life," said Michael Benabib, 64, who picked up two bananas. "This is the real neighborhood," he said. "Just people and families. We will miss you."

An Upper West Side institution that has served generations of shoppers, Zingone Bros. market — all 25 by 75 feet of it — plans to close. The old-time grocery is shuttering partly due to an inheritance dispute among family members who co-own the store and because one of the co-owners now wants to retire.

In 2025, Gabriella Vinci, the great-granddaughter of one of the store's founders, filed a lawsuit in New York State Court seeking to compel the sale of the building that houses the store and rent-stabilized apartments. Vinci inherited a 25% stake in the building following her mother's death.
Family members opposing the sale bemoaned, in a court filing, that it would "destroy a longstanding family business, and eliminate a family legacy spanning nearly fifty (50) years."

The Zingones received last minute offers of financial help "from generous people in the neighborhood," said Richie Zingone, Nicholas's son. "It opened the door, but I don't think it's possible anymore."

The closure, coming not long after Thanksgiving, will mark the latest loss of a family-run business in a city that, like many across the country, has seen chains proliferate, without the close, personal connections to customers that neighborhood fixtures like Zingone Bros. have built over generations.

As word of its impending demise has spread, Zingone regulars have been stopping by to make their purchases and pay their respects to Nicholas, who still comes to the store every day, as well as to his sons and nephew. Many of the customers had tears in their eyes.
Michael Weaver, a customer for 47 years, said the Zingones had more than once lent $20 to his children when they were teenagers and he and his wife were away.

"I feel, and my wife feels, like we've learned that a close friend is terminally ill with this closing," said Weaver, who stopped by the store this week to pick up onions, carrots, potatoes and other Thanksgiving items as well as cereal, fruit and milk for his visiting grandchildren.
Zingone Bros. belongs to another retail era, a period well before superstores and discounters, when delis, groceries and other shops were family businesses and neighborhood staples.
Brothers Domenico and Vincenzo Zingone started their namesake grocer in 1927. Initially they split the small space with a local butcher, then took over the full store when the butcher retired.
Its accordion doors took in the breezes coursing down Columbus Avenue, cooling the store in the summer while turning it so cold during the winter that icicles formed inside.

The store served neighborhood residents, as well as commuters heading to the Bronx. Customers would call in their orders. They grew close to the Zingones. Richie Zingone recalled one customer joining his mother Evelyn in the delivery room for the birth of his first child.

For decades, the family rented the space. Nicholas Zingone and his cousin Ralph, the second-generation owners, took out a $25,000 mortgage as a downpayment on the building in 1975, before the neighborhood gentrified and property values soared.
Their ownership of the building insulated Zingone Bros. from the fate of many family-run businesses. Those businesses have dwindled as neighborhoods gentrify and rents rise.
After weathering the Great Depression, the Zingones prospered through recessions and the pandemic, when family members packed bags of groceries for deliveries or for customers to pick up.
"I would write a list, walk by, hand it to them and pick it up either that afternoon or a couple of days later," said Richard Jaffe, a customer for 35 years.
Among the regulars who had house accounts allowing them to pay on credit, Richie Zingone said, were Jerry and Jessica Seinfeld, Leonard Bernstein, Peter Jennings, Jane Pauley and Matt Dillon.
John McEnroe picked Christmas trees from the yard behind the store, before the Zingones stopped selling them a decade ago.

Recently the store was featured in Olivia Rodrigo's "stupid song" music video. While singing about the inadequacy of love songs, Rodrigo danced on the checkerboard tiles between bags of flour and tubs of Greek yogurt.
What ultimately sealed the fate of Zingone's was another factor in the demise of many family-run businesses: the challenge of transitioning from one generation to the next.

Thirty percent of family-owned businesses make it to the second generation, and 13% are owned by family through the third generation, according to a study that tracked 200 Illinois manufacturers between 1924 and 1984.

"When a business is smaller, it puts more pressure on the business to sustain itself financially and the relationships of those people involved," said Kristi Daeda, chief executive of the Family Business Consulting Group.
In the Zingones' case, Vinci, the granddaughter of Nicholas's brother Ralph Zingone, is seeking to cash out. "My client is looking for an amicable resolution with her family," Vinci's lawyer said.

Nicholas and his sons Richie and Nicholas Anthony, also known as Nick Jr., would like to keep the business open, but can't afford to buy out their cousins or invest the money needed to modernize the store and hire new staff, Nicholas Anthony said.

Also, Nicholas Anthony, 55, doesn't want his children, ages 16 and 18, to work for the business when he retires. "It's twelve hour days, six days a week," he said. "I don't want to put my children in the same position."
Dominick, 66, Ralph's son and another owner of the business, filled potato bins and shined cucumbers with olive oil as a child working at the store.
"After 40 years," he said, "I'm ready to retire."
